script:
By now, you've probably heard that seed oils are basically toxic sludge.
That cooking with canola or soybean oil quietly destroys your health.
The theory actually sounds convincing at first.
Seed oils are high in an omega-6 fat called linoleic acid.
The claim is that your body converts it into arachidonic acid, which drives up inflammation.
Sounds scary, right?
Except human clinical trials tell a completely different story.
In human trials, increasing linoleic acid by up to six times
didn't significantly increase arachidonic acid in human tissues.
And across fifteen randomized controlled trials,
varying linoleic acid had zero effect on inflammatory markers like CRP.
In fact, across thirty studies following over sixty-eight thousand people,
higher levels were linked to a lower risk of stroke,
and a thirty-five percent lower risk of type two diabetes.
So why does everyone blame seed oils for everything?
On average, Americans consume over forty grams of vegetable oil a day.
That's about three tablespoons.
And almost none of that comes from sautéing vegetables at home.
More than half the calories Americans eat at home come from ultra-processed food.
Seed oils hide in chips, cookies, and fryers where oil gets repeatedly reheated.
Those foods are packed with sugar, sodium, and tons of extra calories.
Eating that all day will wreck your health, but not because the oil is toxic.
Now, I'm not calling seed oils healthy just because they aren't toxic.
It depends, and the dose makes the poison.
Your problem was never the tablespoon of oil in your skillet.
It was the ultra-processed diet it was riding in on.

sources.supports: Seed oils contain linoleic acid, an essential omega-6 fatty acid; in a study of over 68,000 participants across 30 studies in 13 countries, higher linoleic acid levels were associated with a lower risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease; participants with the highest linoleic acid levels had a 35% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes; more than half of calories U.S. adults consume at home come from ultra-processed foods, which are high in added sugar, sodium, and calories; seed oils have been demonized because their effects are conflated with the ultra-processed foods they are used in.

Vegetable oils such as soy and canola are rich in linoleic acid; the common concern is that dietary linoleic acid converts to arachidonic acid and causes inflammation; a systematic review of 15 randomized controlled trials found varying linoleic acid intake had no significant effect on circulating C-reactive protein (CRP) or other inflammatory markers; Americans consume an average of over 40 grams (around 3 tablespoons) of vegetable oil each day.
A systematic review of human clinical trials showed that increasing dietary linoleic acid up to sixfold did not significantly increase arachidonic acid content in human tissue or blood phospholipids.

Social media claims label seed oils like canola and soybean oil as toxic and inflammatory; the claim that dietary linoleic acid drives inflammation is not supported by human blood marker research; seed oils in the diet mostly hide in packaged snack foods like chips, crackers, and cookies, and deep-fried restaurant fast foods where oil is repeatedly reheated to high temperatures; using a few tablespoons of seed oil to sauté vegetables at home is healthy; health outcomes depend on overall diet and consuming fat in moderation.
